Nearly every good you buy was ultimately delivered to its end point by truck, and trucks move roughly 72% of U.S. freight by weight, so a diesel spike becomes a cost increase embedded in everything on the shelf. 

The pass-through is fast because most carrier fuel surcharges are indexed directly to this exact EIA weekly average. When this number moves, freight invoices reset within days, and those costs flow into wholesale prices and then onto retail shelves over the following weeks.

The Midwest jumped 43 cents in one week to $6.68 a gallon, and that is important because it is where grain, fertilizer, and farm equipment move. Food input costs will feel this well before the CPI report shows it.

Companies now have two choices: raise prices or absorb the hit to margins. Either way someone pays, and the Fed is staring at a goods inflation impulse that rate policy cannot fix.
